title: Animals get food by eating
learning_goal_display: I can explain that animals get food by eating, and plants can make their own food.

source_provenance.objective_verbatim: Explain that animals cannot make their own food; they get it from what they eat.

ta_brief_html:
Full staff brief

Science book routine and adult support

Beside the You do, mark I (independent), S (supported) or C (choice): the level of independence, not the effort.

Give time to start → point to the relevant place → rephrase → offer a small prompt or word bank → reduce to a limited choice. Never straight to telling the answer.

No cold calling; nobody is asked to read difficult text aloud.

Tell the teacher the barrier: reading, vocabulary, processing, regulation, writing or a science misconception. Avoid prompting through every question or dictating the final answer.

E Evidence on the school's evidence app

Lean capture on the school's evidence app (E): 30-second clip, photo, or one-line context note.

Point, sign, repeat after the adult, demonstrate, a clip on the school's evidence app, choice board.

If behind

A pupil who missed last lesson: give the Arrival reminders and today's must-know words, not the missed lesson's work.

Arrival and Starter

Arrival 1: Where does a rabbit get its food: eating grass or making it? Answer: Eating grass.

Arrival 2: Name one plant in a food chain. Answer: For example, grass.

Arrival 3: Name one job food does in a body. Answer: It provides energy or materials for growth.

Arrival 4: Do muscles pull or push bones? Answer: Pull.

Starter: A plant and rabbit both need energy. Which can make its own food?

You do routes

Independent is the preferred route: the task is completed in the book without answer-giving support. Supported uses a small nearby prompt; Choice uses limited options and a short scientific sentence, label or reason.

Choice: Choose grass or stone for a rabbit’s food. Match rabbit to grass and fox to rabbit. In your book, draw one chain and finish: The rabbit gets food by eating ____.

Practical method and access

Photograph the practical at the planned point, upload it to the school's evidence app with this code, and stick a copy in the book.

Lesson code: SCI-BUILD-A1-W08-P1

Method strip · stick in your book
  1. Set out only the printed organism cards and paper arrows; do not handle or feed real organisms.
  2. Match the animal-food pairs and ask the adult to check the card setup. STOP AND CHECK with the adult before continuing.
  3. Build both supplied chains with arrows from food to eater.
  4. Repair the reversed arrow, then cover one plant card.
  5. Record one feeding-link observation and explain one possible effect of fewer plants, with one model limit.

Only the apparatus for the current stage goes on the table. If safe participation is not possible, watch the teacher demonstration and record an observation and one conclusion in your book.

After the practical, record what you observed and one conclusion linked to today’s learning goal. Add a method or diagram only where it is part of the learning.

Planned photograph point: after the observation is recorded and before the pupil writes the conclusion. Model evidence is identified as model evidence; it never proves independent practical completion.

P17 · SLT planning and evaluation

Lesson code: SCI-BUILD-A1-W08-P1

SoW reference: BUILD scheme of work, Autumn 1 return week

Exact SoW outcome: Explain that animals cannot make their own food; they get it from what they eat.

Evidence (scheme of work): Pearson Entry Level Science 8939; AQA UAS science units. Observation, results and end-of-unit evidence.

Evidence in this lesson: Two labelled chains, a repaired arrow, one cautious prediction and one model limit.

Evidence location: Book under the strip; record exact spoken or pointed responses with actual support. Genuine physical records remain linked to their original method.

Label evidence on the school's evidence app with this code: SCI-BUILD-A1-W08-P1. Model data is analysis only; never log it as practical completion.

Stage plan and staff moves

Stage and MinutesTaskStaff move

Cover a plant, then explain what could change and one model limit.One adult supports pupils needing the Supported route; the other holds the group. Swap deployment across the week. Scaffold only the step that is blocked.
Review and improve · 3 minCheck your evidence, hear one next step and improve one part.Give private VF and one precise NS+. Keep pupil ownership; record R only after response to a real next step and genuine adult Audience.

Planned adaptations

Cognition and learning: Arrival: offer two clues; I do: one step at a time; independent: keep the evidence card visible and fade the first prompt no longer needed.

Communication and interaction: Hinge and evidence desk: rehearse one response, wait, then accept pointing, signing, speech, symbol, drawing or exact-word scribing.

SEMH: Arrival and review: familiar adult, private check-in, predictable first–then cue, agreed pause and quiet re-entry; one neutral next step.

Sensory and physical: Evidence desk and independent: low-density cards, no-touch/director route, accessible position and larger visual; staff handle equipment when required.

EAL: Model and independent: explain the everyday bridge alongside the scientific word, allow first-language planning, then rehearse the relevant because statement.

EEF five-a-day: explicit instruction, cognitive/metacognitive strategies, scaffolding, flexible grouping and appropriate technology. Apply the lowest effective prompt; fade as independence returns. After teaching, confirm the planned adaptations actually used.

Adult deployment and feedback

Independent: one adult holds the group, one supports the selected pupils; swap across the week. Use VF · WS · I · NS+ · E · R · // · ? privately. R requires a real next-step response and genuine Audience; do not add it automatically.

If behind

Must teach core: A green plant is a producer: it makes food using light. An animal is a consumer: it eats to obtain food.

Shorten or merge: reduce the number of similar evidence cards; retain the hinge, one independent reason and the exit.

Dependency: use the exit to choose retrieval or a new application; do not assume attendance establishes coverage.

Practical safety and access

Do not collect, handle or feed real plants or animals. Use non-graphic examples. Avoid personal food discussion.

Prepare both chain sets and feeding clue cards. Check what was taught before choosing how much modelling to use.

Cards and models only; no live feeding or handling.

Apply the current school-approved risk assessment and equipment instructions. Supplied model records are labelled illustrative, not measured pupil results.

First lesson back staff card

Before the lesson, scan the books for five minutes. Ask the cover teacher and TAs what was taught. Check the roll against the books. Existing NS+ is history: begin fresh feedback. After the check, one read, once, to shape Autumn 2.

Use the book scan once to choose this lesson’s route. Welcome the pupil at their actual starting point. No judgement about missed teaching or duplicate recording.

Answers and accepted reasoning

  • The plant makes food using light; the animals get food by eating.
  • A simple model suggests a possible change. Other food sources and links can matter.
  • Food passes from grass to rabbit to fox.
  • Food passes from leaves to caterpillar to robin.
  • Repair to grass → rabbit → fox. Read each arrow as is eaten by.
  • Animals obtain food by eating. Green plants can make their own food using light.
  • Cow → eats grass: the animal obtains food by eating. In a chain, grass points towards the cow.
  • The owl obtains food by eating a small animal; this is an example, not every owl’s complete diet.
  • Exit: grass is the producer. The arrow means is eaten by; food/energy passes to the eater. Both chains begin with a green plant that makes food using light. Animals obtain food by eating. Fewer plants may affect consumers indirectly; other feeding links mean exact numbers cannot be inferred.
  • The leaves are part of the green producer plant, not a separate species. Green plants in these examples make food using light; roots take in water and minerals, not ready-made food. Sunlight supplies energy but is not an edible organism. Producer does not mean every producer must be a plant. Animals obtaining food here is a biological idea, not a claim about human cooking. A paper cover supports a qualified prediction, not ecological measurements. A photograph alone does not establish understanding, and no photography or public sharing is required.
